abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by skin and internal organ fibrosis, vasculopathy and immune dysregulation. Skin fibrosis, commonly assessed using the modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS), remains a defining feature of SSc and is associated with disease severity and prognosis. However, conventional clinical assessment provides limited insight into the molecular heterogeneity underlying cutaneous involvement. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have shown that SSc skin contains distinct fibroblast states, immune-stromal interactions and spatially organized fibrotic niches. These data challenge the view of cutaneous fibrosis as a uniform process and instead support a model in which different cellular and spatial programmes may contribute to clinically similar patterns of skin involvement. In this review, we synthesize the findings from single-cell and spatial multi-omics studies of SSc skin published between 2021 and 2025, examine the extent to which molecular heterogeneity relates to clinical phenotype, and discuss the implications for cutaneous assessment, treatment response heterogeneity and biologically informed patient subgrouping. Because skin biopsy is clinically accessible and can be repeated over time, it provides a practical setting in which these molecular observations can be studied. Whether they improve patient stratification, treatment selection or cutaneous outcome assessment will depend on prospective validation in larger and clinically well-characterized cohorts.

sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune disease. Autoimmune diseases are conditions where the immune system attacks a person’s healthy cells and tissues by mistake. SSc can cause hardening and scarring of the skin and some internal organs. Skin thickening is one of its most significant symptoms. It is measured using the ‘modified Rodnan skin score’ (mRSS). However, people with similar skin scores may still have important differences taking place in the skin. This suggests that skin tissue could be used to assess how severe the disease is. It could also be used to better classify people with the condition. We discuss the results of studies published between 2021 and 2025. The studies used modern analytical methods to investigate skin in people with SSc. These methods examine skin tissue cell by cell. Some studies also show where these cells sit within the skin. The methods can identify different cell types, show how they interact with each other and show where they are located in diseased skin. The findings show that the condition does not look the same in every person or in every part of the skin. They also help explain why the usual ways of measuring disease (like the mRSS) may not fully reflect the underlying biology of the disease. In future, this may help researchers group patients more accurately and design better ways to measure skin disease in clinical trials. However, further studies are needed before these approaches can be used in routine clinical practice.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
